intro: The chorus that closes Part II alternates three kinds of speech: a tune sung together, a line passed between voices, and long notes held above moving counterpoint. Its force comes from those changes of texture, not from singing everything loudly.
question: How does a chorus gain force without simply singing louder?

sections.label: Closing cadence · approximate
sections.mNote: acclamation gathers into longer chords around a general pause

cues.title: Together and in pursuit
cues.text: Throughout the chorus, distinguish voices moving together from lines that enter one after another. Handel varies the force of a declaration by changing its texture, not only the weight of the sound.
cues.evidence: The score alternates chordal declarations with imitative writing. This is a whole-chorus listening guide; no sung word or individual entrance is assigned to this timestamp.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Jennens supplies the words
cues.text: Charles Jennens assembled the scriptural text that Handel set in 1741. The three parts do not enact one continuous plot: they move from prophecy and birth through suffering and resurrection to the believer’s response.
cues.evidence: Teresa M. Neff’s Handel and Haydn Society programme note describes Jennens’s compilation and the three-part design. https://handelandhaydn.org/interactive-program-notes-handels-messiah/

cues.title: Withdrawal and renewed weight
cues.text: Across this stretch, the sound falls back before another stronger passage. Listen for changes in how the voices combine, without assuming that a larger sound must mean a new melody.
cues.evidence: Relative level drops around 1:10 and rises again around 1:20. The analysis supports this contrast but does not identify the words or separate the choral lines.

cues.title: A Dublin charitable benefit
cues.text: Messiah was first performed at the Music Hall in Fishamble Street, Dublin, on 13 April 1742. London heard it in 1743. Its first public setting was a charitable concert, not a church service.
cues.evidence: Neff’s programme note documents the Dublin venue, date and charitable purpose, followed by the London performances. https://handelandhaydn.org/interactive-program-notes-handels-messiah/

cues.title: Long notes against short
cues.text: Listen through the later part of the chorus for sustained notes against moving figures. A held line can continue a proclamation while other voices repeat and develop their own material.
cues.evidence: This is a score-informed description of the chorus’s layered writing. The strong recorded region around 2:00–2:15 does not by itself locate a particular sung phrase.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The Foundling performances
cues.text: A 1750 performance of Messiah benefited London’s Foundling Hospital. Annual performances followed, helping establish the work as a recurring public event as well as a source of charitable income.
cues.evidence: Neff dates the Foundling Hospital Messiah benefit to 1750 and describes the ensuing annual performances. https://handelandhaydn.org/interactive-program-notes-handels-messiah/

cues.title: Space at the close
cues.text: Across the closing passage, attend to the spacing of the final gestures and the resonance after them. Withholding a new attack can give an ending weight without adding more notes.
cues.evidence: Detected attacks become sparse around 3:05–3:15, followed by a sharp decay by 3:20. The report cannot identify the exact timing of the final word.

transitions.title: One declaration becomes several pursuing voices
transitions.how: The opening’s block-like acclamations give way to overlapping entries on “For the Lord God omnipotent reigneth”. The short “Hallelujah” rhythm remains available as an answer, so the new texture does not discard the opening. D major and its A-major dominant provide the harmonic frame; the bass now participates in the exchanges rather than merely underpinning a unanimous chord. Handel keeps the Allegro pulse while changing how many different stages of a phrase can be heard together.
transitions.evidence: The contrasting-textures marker is 0:36, also a measured boundary between A- and D-centred windows. The score supplies the alternation of acclamation and imitative “For the Lord” writing. The words identify the passage’s material, not an entrance at 0:36; the relation study explicitly withholds exact sung-word and fugal-entry timings.

transitions.title: A rising subject keeps the proclamation moving
transitions.how: After the more chordal proclamation, “And he shall reign” supplies a rising subject that can enter in successive voices. An entry on the tonic side is answered on the dominant side, linking D major with A rather than requiring a new principal key. The bass becomes a melodic participant, and the shorter “for ever” figures continue beneath later entries. Growth comes from overlapping phrase beginnings, with the orchestral pulse carrying across the join.
transitions.evidence: The central-build boundary is 1:44; the analysis marks a change there and a further rise towards 1:55–2:15. The score’s imitative “And he shall reign” subject and its tonic/dominant relationship supply the explanation. The text describes the surrounding contrapuntal stretch, not the timing of its first bass entry.

transitions.title: Held notes rise above the moving voices
transitions.how: The counterpoint does not simply stop for “King of kings”. Long upper notes are laid above the shorter “for ever” and “Hallelujah” figures, then the sustained proclamation is repeated higher. Changing bass harmonies support that ascent while the lower voices keep moving. Handel makes register and note length do the work of a crescendo: the ear follows a rising ceiling above the continuing rhythmic material, before the parts gather again around D major.
transitions.evidence: The later-proclamations marker is approximately 2:18, after measured boundaries at 1:58, 2:04, 2:10 and 2:14. The score supplies the ascending long-note proclamations over moving counterpoint. The report’s strongest region around 2:10–2:15 helps locate the broader build, but neither words nor each successive pitch are aligned.

transitions.title: The moving parts agree, then wait
transitions.how: The separate choral lines converge on repeated “Hallelujah” chords. Quicker motion is stripped away, and a general pause separates the final declaration from the accumulated repetitions. Its longer note values make the familiar word sound different without introducing a new theme. G-major subdominant harmony resolves to D major in the concluding plagal cadence; the bass and the gathered choral parts confirm the same tonic after the silence.
transitions.evidence: The closing-cadence marker is approximately 3:06, a measured boundary; attacks become sparse in the 3:05–3:15 windows before the final decay. The score supplies the convergence, rest, longer final declaration and G-to-D plagal close. A closing score excerpt is reproduced at https://www.pianotv.net/2017/12/handel-messiah-hallelujah-chorus/. The silence itself is not timed to the section marker.

facts: With Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; theatre work in Hamburg; study and commissions in Italy, 1706–10
Hanover briefly; settled in London in 1712; became a British subject in 1727
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos, chamber cantatas and ceremonial orchestral music
composer.background:
Handel grew up in Halle, the son of a barber-surgeon, and studied with Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow, organist of the town’s principal church. Zachow’s teaching included counterpoint, keyboard playing and the copying of other composers’ music. Handel briefly enrolled at the university and held an organist’s post before moving to Hamburg in 1703. Its public opera house offered a different education: he played in the orchestra and encountered the practical demands of singers, stage machinery and mixed theatrical repertory. His first opera, Almira, was performed there in 1705, with a German text incorporating Italian arias.

From 1706 to 1710 Handel worked in Italy, writing cantatas, sacred music and opera for patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Rome gave him access to virtuoso singers and to instrumentalists associated with Corelli. The Latin Dixit Dominus of 1707 demands rapid, independent choral lines and sustained control of dissonance; the chamber cantatas make emotional turns within much smaller forces. Agrippina, performed in Venice at the end of 1709, assembles much previously written material into a calculated theatrical comedy. Reuse was already part of his method: a successful musical gesture could acquire a different function when assigned to a new character and situation.
composer.epithet: A German-trained composer of Italian opera who made the English chorus an actor in public musical drama.
